name: Boudhanath
tagline: The great white stupa where Tibet meets the Kathmandu Valley
meta_description: Boudhanath with locals: dawn kora round the great stupa, monastery puja, thangka studios, Kopan, Tibetan food and where to stay in Boudha, Kathmandu.
summary: Boudhanath, Boudha for short, is one of the largest stupas in South Asia and the centre of Tibetan Buddhist life in Nepal, 7 km north-east of Thamel. Walk the clockwise kora at dawn or dusk, visit a monastery puja, and eat Tibetan food. Half a day is enough; a night here is better.
intro: You enter Boudha through a gateway off a loud main road, and the noise drops away. In front of you is a vast white dome, its gilded tower painted with the watchful eyes of the Buddha, strung with lines of prayer flags. Round it flows a steady river of people walking clockwise: Tibetan grandmothers with prayer wheels and beads, monks in maroon, Sherpa families, Newar neighbours, tourists trying to keep pace.

The stupa stood on the old trade route from Tibet, which entered the valley via Sankhu, and Tibetan traders and pilgrims stopped here for centuries. After 1959, when thousands of Tibetans fled into exile, many settled round Boudha. Dozens of monasteries have been built since, and the area has become the main centre of Tibetan Buddhism in Nepal, with schools, thangka studios and shops selling butter lamps, incense and robes.

The best times are early morning and evening, when the kora is busiest and the light softest. In the middle of the day it is quieter and easier to climb onto the stupa's lower terraces and to visit monasteries in the side lanes. On Losar, the Tibetan new year, and the full moons of the Tibetan calendar, Boudha fills to the edges with pilgrims.

story.title: A stupa on the road to Lhasa
paras: Nobody knows exactly when Boudhanath was first built. Newar chronicles link it to the Licchavi kings of the first millennium, and Tibetan tradition tells of its building by a poultry keeper's widow and her sons. What is clear is that it sat on the main trade route between the valley and Tibet, and that for centuries Tibetan traders, pilgrims and lamas stopped here to pray for a safe crossing of the Himalaya.

Until the mid-20th century, Boudha was a small village in fields, with a few Tibetan and Sherpa families and a lama who cared for the stupa. Everything changed after 1959. Tibetan refugees settled here, and from the late 1960s monasteries of all the main schools of Tibetan Buddhism were founded round the stupa, often by lamas who had escaped. The village became a town of monks, traders, artists and students from across the world.

The April 2015 earthquake cracked the harmika, the square section bearing the painted eyes, and the spire. The upper part was taken down and rebuilt with gilded copper, funded largely by donations from Buddhist devotees, and the stupa was reconsecrated in November 2016. Today the circuit is busier than ever, with new homes for Tibetan, Sherpa and Himalayan families rising in every direction.

legend: In the Tibetan telling, a poultry keeper's widow asked the king for as much land as a buffalo hide would cover to build a stupa. The king agreed. She cut the hide into thin strips and laid them round a large plot. When officials complained, the king replied that he had given his word and could not take it back: jarung khashor, permission once given cannot be withdrawn. The stupa still carries that name in Tibetan.
people: Boudha is home to Tibetan families who came after 1959 and their children and grandchildren born in Nepal, along with Sherpa, Tamang, Hyolmo and other Himalayan Buddhist communities. Hundreds of monks and nuns study in the monasteries. Newar and Brahmin-Chhetri families lived here before them and still own many houses. Tibetan, Nepali, Sherpa and English are all heard on the kora.

untold.fact: Boudhanath lies on the old trade route from Tibet, which entered the Kathmandu Valley through the village of Sankhu to the north-east. Tibetan merchants traditionally stopped at the stupa to pray before and after the journey across the Himalaya.
The stupa's Tibetan name, Jarung Khashor, refers to a legend of permission given that could not be taken back. Its Newar name is Khasti, and the Nepali name Boudhanath means lord of wisdom.

After the 2015 earthquake damaged its upper section, the harmika and spire of Boudhanath were removed and rebuilt, largely funded by Buddhist donors rather than the state, and the stupa reopened in November 2016.

taste.name: Laphing and butter tea
taste.text: Laphing is a cold, slippery mung-bean noodle served with chilli, garlic and vinegar, sold from small stalls and hole-in-the-wall shops in the lanes off the stupa. Wash it down with po cha, salty Tibetan butter tea, or sweet milk tea, in a family-run Tibetan restaurant facing the kora.

facts: Great stupa, Tibetan monasteries, kora, thangka

highlights.title: The dawn and dusk kora
highlights.text: Join the clockwise walk round the stupa from about 5.30 am or after 5 pm, when Tibetan families, monks and neighbours circle with prayer wheels and malas. Three circuits take about 30 minutes.

highlights.title: The stupa terraces
highlights.text: Climb the steps onto the lower terraces of the stupa itself for a closer look at the dome, the prayer wheels and the painted eyes above. It is quieter here at midday, and you can sit for a while.

highlights.title: Monastery puja
highlights.text: In the mornings and late afternoons, monks in the larger gompas chant prayers to drums, horns and cymbals. Visitors may sit quietly at the back of most halls. Remove shoes and walk clockwise inside.

highlights.title: Thangka studios
highlights.text: Painters in studios round the stupa grind mineral pigments and work for weeks on detailed Buddhist scroll paintings. Many welcome visitors to watch, and explain how the iconography is set by strict rules.

highlights.title: Rooftop views
highlights.text: Several cafes and restaurants on the circle have rooftops facing the eyes of the stupa. Come for tea at sunset, when butter lamps are lit in the small shrine at the base and the crowd on the kora thickens.

highlights.title: Kopan Monastery
highlights.text: On a hill about 3 km north, Kopan is known for its meditation courses for visitors and its views over the valley. Walk up through fields and houses, or take a taxi up and walk back down.

how_to_reach.text: Boudha is about 7 km from Thamel and 3 km from the airport. A taxi or ride-hailing car takes 20 to 40 minutes from Thamel depending on traffic on the ring road. Microbuses from Ratnapark run to Chabahil and Boudha. The stupa is reached through gates on the main road; cars cannot enter the circle.

From Pashupatinath, a 30 to 40 minute walk north-east through Gaushala and Chabahil leads to Boudha, passing the old Chabahil stupa. It is a good way to link the two sites on one day, ideally finishing with the evening kora.

where_to_stay: Staying in Boudha means being on the kora at dawn before the city wakes. Monastery guesthouses and small family hotels line the lanes north of the stupa, with simple, clean rooms. Mid-range hotels sit on the roads behind the circle. Dwarika's Hotel at Battisputali, between Boudha and Pashupatinath, is about 15 minutes away by car. Gokarna Forest Resort, 20 minutes north-east, is a quiet base for both.
tips: Always walk clockwise round the stupa and any chorten or prayer wheel.
Foreign visitors pay a small entry fee at the gates; keep the ticket if you plan to come and go.
Do not touch monks' heads or sit with your feet pointing at an altar in a monastery hall.
Butter lamps can be lit for a small donation at the shrine at the stupa's base.
On Losar and full-moon days, the circle is very crowded; come early or late.

experiences.title: Dawn kora with the pilgrims of Boudha
experiences.summary: Walk three slow circuits round the great stupa at first light with Tibetan families, monks and neighbours. We explain the prayer wheels, the eyes, the mantras and the shrines on the way, then sit for butter tea on a rooftop as the sun reaches the dome.
body: By 5.30 am in autumn, the kora is already moving. Elderly Tibetans walk with wooden prayer wheels in one hand and beads in the other, murmuring Om mani padme hum. Some prostrate their way round the circle, sliding forward on wooden hand pads. Monks walk briskly to morning puja. We join the flow and walk at its pace, always clockwise.

On the way we stop at the shrine of Ajima, a goddess honoured at the stupa's base, at the rows of prayer wheels set in the stupa wall, and at the gates of monasteries opening for the day. We explain the stupa's structure: the plinth, dome, harmika with eyes, thirteen steps to enlightenment, and the gilded spire.

After three circuits we climb to a rooftop cafe for po cha, salty Tibetan butter tea, or sweet milk tea, and watch the sun strike the dome and the crowd below grow. It is one of the calmest ways to start a day in Kathmandu, and a good first morning after a long flight.

faqs.q: What is a kora at Boudhanath?
faqs.a: A kora is a clockwise walk round a sacred site, done as a form of prayer and merit. At Boudhanath, pilgrims circle the stupa repeatedly, turning prayer wheels and reciting mantras. Visitors are welcome to join; just walk clockwise, at an easy pace, and do not stop suddenly in the flow.

faqs.q: What time should I go to Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Go early, from about 5.30 to 7.30 am, or in the evening after 5 pm. These are the busiest times on the kora with local pilgrims, and the light is soft. Midday is quieter and good for climbing onto the stupa's terraces and visiting monasteries.

faqs.q: How much is the Boudhanath entry fee?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay a small entry fee, a few hundred rupees, at the gates on the main road; SAARC nationals pay less. The ticket lets you walk the kora and climb the terraces. Fees change, so check current status before you travel and carry rupees in cash.

experiences.title: Sit in on a Tibetan monastery puja
experiences.summary: Visit two of Boudha's monasteries during prayers: deep chanting, long horns, drums and butter lamps. We explain the main images, the murals and the daily life of the monks, and how the monasteries came to Boudha after 1959.
body: Boudha has monasteries of all the main Tibetan Buddhist schools, many founded in the 1960s and 1970s by lamas who left Tibet. We visit two that welcome respectful visitors at prayer times, such as Shechen Tennyi Dargyeling or Ka-Nying Shedrub Ling, depending on the day's schedule.

In the prayer hall, rows of monks sit facing each other, chanting from long loose-leaf texts. Every so often the chant is broken by long copper horns, oboe-like gyaling, cymbals and drums. Visitors sit at the back on a cushion or bench. We explain in whispers what is happening, or wait outside to talk.

Afterwards we walk round the hall to look at the main images, usually the Buddha, Padmasambhava and protector deities, and the murals that cover the walls. If a monk has time, we ask about his day, which often starts before 5 am. We also explain how young monks are educated, and how monasteries are funded.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit monasteries in Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Yes. Most larger monasteries in Boudha welcome visitors outside private ceremonies. Remove shoes before entering the prayer hall, walk clockwise, sit at the back during puja, and do not point your feet at the altar. Ask before taking photographs; some halls do not allow them during prayers.

faqs.q: What time are prayers at Boudhanath monasteries?
faqs.a: Times vary by monastery, but morning prayers usually begin early, before or around 6 am, and afternoon prayers between about 3 and 5 pm. Special pujas happen on full-moon days and festivals. Your guide will check the day's schedule, since visits are best timed to a session.

faqs.q: What should I wear to a monastery in Nepal?
faqs.a: Wear clothes that cover shoulders and knees, and shoes that are easy to take off. Avoid hats inside halls. Leather items are fine in most Tibetan monasteries. A small scarf is useful in cold halls in winter. Dress modestly rather than formally.

experiences.title: Watch thangka painters at work in Boudha
experiences.summary: Visit a working thangka studio near the stupa where painters grind mineral pigments and paint Buddhist scrolls by hand. Learn how the grid of proportions works, what each deity means and how to tell a hand-painted thangka from a print.
body: Thangkas are Buddhist scroll paintings used in meditation and ritual. Around Boudha, studios employ Tibetan, Tamang, Gurung and Newar painters who trained for years under masters. We visit a studio where artists work on cotton canvas, stretched on wooden frames, bent close with fine brushes.

A senior painter shows how a thangka begins: the canvas is primed and polished, a strict grid of proportions is laid out for the deity, and the drawing is built up line by line. Colours come from ground minerals and plants mixed with glue, and gold is applied as a paste and then burnished. A large, detailed thangka can take months.

We discuss the main subjects, such as the Wheel of Life, mandalas, the Medicine Buddha and Green Tara, and how to judge quality: fine faces, even shading, crisp gold lines. There is no obligation to buy. If you do, ask who painted it, how long it took, and for a receipt.

faqs.q: How much does a real thangka cost in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Small hand-painted thangkas start at around USD 50 to 150, while large, highly detailed pieces with real gold by master painters can cost several thousand. Very cheap thangkas are often printed or quickly painted. Ask to see the studio and the painter, and compare a few shops before buying.

faqs.q: How can I tell a hand-painted thangka?
faqs.a: Look closely: hand-painted thangkas have slight brush marks, layered colour and fine, raised gold lines. Prints look flat and uniform under a magnifier. Faces and eyes are the hardest part and show the painter's skill. A genuine studio will happily explain and show unfinished work.

faqs.q: Can I learn thangka painting in Boudha?
faqs.a: Some studios offer short introductory sessions or longer courses for visitors willing to commit weeks or months. A short session teaches basic proportions and line work. Contact studios in advance; we can arrange an introduction to a painter who teaches visitors.

experiences.title: Walk up to Kopan for quiet and valley views
experiences.summary: A gentle walk from the stupa up to Kopan Monastery on its hill north of Boudha, through lanes and fields. Visit the gardens and main hall, look out over the valley, and, if the timing fits, join a short introduction to meditation offered to visitors.
body: From the north side of the stupa, lanes lead uphill past new houses, small gompas and the odd field of vegetables. In about 45 minutes to an hour you reach Kopan, a monastery and nunnery on a hilltop at around 1,400 m. It is known around the world for its meditation and Buddhism courses for foreigners, which have run for decades.

Visitors are welcome in the grounds during set hours. We walk through gardens of stupas and prayer flags, look into the main gompa with its large statues, and stop at the viewpoint over the valley. On clear days, the hills of Shivapuri and Nagarjun frame the city, and the white dome of Boudha shines below.

Kopan runs regular courses and sometimes short drop-in sessions; we check what is on and help you book if you want to stay longer. Otherwise, sit quietly for a while, have tea in the canteen if it is open, and walk back down to Boudha for lunch.

faqs.q: Can I visit Kopan Monastery without staying?
faqs.a: Yes. Kopan welcomes day visitors to the grounds during set hours, usually mornings and early afternoons, though it may close to visitors during courses and retreats. Dress modestly, keep quiet near study halls and check the current visitor schedule before you go.

faqs.q: How do I get to Kopan Monastery from Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Walk about 3 km north through lanes and fields, which takes 45 minutes to an hour uphill, or take a taxi for 10 to 15 minutes. Many people take a taxi up and walk down. Your guide will lead the walking route, which is not well signposted.

faqs.q: Does Kopan offer meditation courses?
faqs.a: Yes. Kopan is well known for its introductory courses on Buddhism and meditation, from a few days to a month, including a long course in November. Places can fill early. Courses are booked directly with the monastery; check dates and rules before you travel.

faqs.q: How old is Boudhanath stupa?
faqs.a: Its exact age is unknown. Newar chronicles link it to the Licchavi period, perhaps the 5th to 7th centuries CE, and it has been rebuilt and enlarged many times. The current upper section dates from the rebuilding after the 2015 earthquake, completed in 2016.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Two to three hours covers the kora, the stupa terraces and one monastery. Half a day lets you add a thangka studio and lunch. To feel the place properly, stay a night nearby and walk the kora at dawn and dusk.

faqs.q: Is Boudhanath the same as the Monkey Temple?
faqs.a: No. Boudhanath is the large white stupa in north-east Kathmandu at the centre of the Tibetan community. The Monkey Temple is Swayambhunath, a stupa on a hill west of the city. Both are Buddhist UNESCO-listed sites, about 30 to 45 minutes apart by car.

faqs.q: Can I visit Boudhanath at night?
faqs.a: Yes. The circle stays open, and evenings are lively with pilgrims on the kora until about 8 pm. Restaurants and shops round the stupa close gradually after that. It is generally safe; take normal care with bags and phones in the crowd.

faqs.q: What is the best day to visit Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Any day works. Full-moon days in the Tibetan calendar, Losar in February or March, and Buddha Jayanti in May bring large crowds, butter lamps and special pujas, which are worth seeing if you do not mind the crowds. Weekday mornings are quietest.

faqs.q: Can I combine Boudhanath and Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Yes. They are about 2 km apart. Visit Pashupatinath in the morning or late afternoon, then walk or drive to Boudha in time for the evening kora. With a guide, the walk via Gaushala and Chabahil takes 30 to 40 minutes.

faqs.q: Is Boudhanath a good place to stay in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want calm and early starts. Boudha is close to the airport, has guesthouses and mid-range hotels, and evenings are peaceful. It is farther from Thamel's restaurants and the old city, about 30 minutes by taxi. It suits spiritual travellers and those heading out early.

faqs.q: Are there rules for visiting Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Walk clockwise round the stupa and inside monasteries, dress modestly, remove shoes in prayer halls, and do not climb on shrines or touch ritual objects. Drones are not allowed. Ask before photographing monks or pilgrims at close range, especially those prostrating.

faqs.q: What can I buy at Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Singing bowls, prayer flags, malas, incense, thangkas, Tibetan carpets and monastic supplies such as robes and butter lamps. Quality varies widely, so compare shops. Thangka studios and the incense shops in the side lanes are better value than stalls on the main circle.
